newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkey's Erbakan clears hurdle but trouble looms.
newsitem.headline: Turkey's Erbakan clears hurdle but trouble looms.

text.p: Turkey's Islamist-led government has cleared the first serious hurdle of its short tenure but looming political and economic problems still threaten its shaky grip on power.

Parliament voted 275 to 256 on Wednesday to reject a motion by the secularist opposition that would have forced Necmettin Erbakan to face a no-confidence vote after little more than 100 days as modern Turkey's first Islamist prime minister.
"Our government has become more powerful," Erbakan told reporters after the vote. "The government is in harmony and will serve the nation until the year 2000," he said.
At the centre of the censure fight was Erbakan's controversial visit 10 days ago to Libya, quarantined by most Western nations for alleged support of terrorism.

But the underlying issue was his broader efforts to redirect Turkish foreign policy away from NATO and the West and toward the Moslem world -- a move that angered secularists at home and alienated long-time patron the United States.

Turkey signed a gas accord with neighbour Iran during an Erbakan visit to Tehran, his first trip abroad as premier. The deal sailed close to a U.S. law banning new energy investment in Iran and Libya.

Erbakan's uneasy coalition with the free-market, pro-Western conservatives of Tansu Ciller's True Path Party, having put the censure attempt behind it, must now grapple with a series of economic and political ills.

Inflation is running at 80 percent, and many bankers and other analysts expect it to burst into triple digits. Huge budget deficits have fed sky-high interest rates, robbing the economy of funds needed for investment.

The Turkish lira has been sinking against the dollar each day. And foreign investors, the World Bank and the International Monetary Fund have all warned of dire consequences if the government does not take matters in hand.
Erbakan has yet to carry out a promise to solve a 12-year-old Kurdish guerrilla conflict through "Moslem brotherhood". More than 20,000 people have died in the fighting.
Disputes with neighbour Greece, over Cyprus and territorial rights in the Aegean Sea, are no nearer to a solution.
Erbakan was pilloried in the media for the Libya fiasco.
Libyan leader Muammar Gaddafi lectured the prime minister on Turkey's treatment of its minority Kurds and its close ties to the West at a joint news conference in Gaddafi's Bedouin tent.
The vote followed almost six hours of often tense debate, with the opposition hammering Erbakan and his Islam-based Welfare Party.
Opposition MPs accused the prime minister of bringing Turkey into disrepute.
"The junior coalition partner is fond of the West, the other partner (Erbakan) cannot take his heart and eyes off the dictatorial regimes of the East," said leftist MP Ismail Cem.

Erbakan's stunned silence in the face of Gaddafi's remarks, as well as his own anti-Western rhetoric while in Libya, provoked a broadside from the United States, which had given him the benefit of the doubt until then.
